reason: The sources provide a detailed account of Yamaguchi's movements, his specific injuries, his dialogue with his supervisor, and his unique legal status, allowing for a compelling narrative.
story: In August 1945, naval engineer Tsutomu Yamaguchi was finishing a business trip in Hiroshima when a flash blinded him. The world's first atomic bomb, Little Boy, detonated just three kilometers away, rupturing his eardrums and searing his skin. Miraculously, he survived and fled to the only place he felt safe: his hometown of Nagasaki. Three days later, wrapped in bandages and shaking with fever, he reported to his office at Mitsubishi. As he described the 'single bomb' that had evaporated Hiroshima, his supervisor scoffed, calling him crazy. At that exact moment, the second atomic bomb, Fat Man, exploded outside the window. Again, Yamaguchi was three kilometers from ground zero. Again, he survived. He became the only person officially recognized by Japan to have survived both attacks, living until age 93 to testify that such horror must never happen a third time.
angle: Tsutomu Yamaguchi was in the middle of telling his boss that a single bomb could destroy an entire city when the second atomic bomb detonated right outside their window.

claims.claim: Tsutomu Yamaguchi is the only person officially recognized by the Japanese government as a survivor of both atomic bombings.
Yamaguchi was a marine engineer for Mitsubishi Heavy Industries.
He was in Hiroshima on a three-month business trip when the first bomb was dropped on August 6, 1945.
The Hiroshima bomb, Little Boy, detonated at 8:15 a.m.
He was approximately 3 kilometers from ground zero during the Hiroshima explosion.
The Hiroshima blast ruptured his eardrums and left him with serious burns on the left side of his upper body.
He spent the night of August 6 in an air-raid shelter in Hiroshima.
Yamaguchi returned to his hometown of Nagasaki on August 8, the day before the second bombing.
Despite his injuries, he reported for work in Nagasaki on the morning of August 9.
He was explaining the Hiroshima explosion to his supervisor when the Nagasaki bomb detonated.
His supervisor interrupted his story to call him crazy or question how one bomb could destroy a city.
The Nagasaki bomb, Fat Man, detonated at 11:02 a.m.
He was approximately 3 kilometers from ground zero during the Nagasaki explosion.
Following the bombings, he suffered from radiation sickness, including a high fever and hair loss.
His wife and young son also survived the Nagasaki bombing.
Yamaguchi worked as a translator for the American occupation forces after the war.
He was officially recognized as a double survivor in March 2009.
He died of stomach cancer on January 4, 2010, at the age of 93.
He spoke at the United Nations in 2006 to advocate for the abolition of nuclear weapons.
Film director James Cameron met with Yamaguchi in 2009 to discuss a project about nuclear weapons.

disputed: Location during Hiroshima blast: S2 mentions a potato field, while S1 and S6 describe him walking toward the docks or office; the script should focus on his distance from ground zero rather than the specific field. Second blast injuries: S2 claims he was knocked unconscious, whereas S1 states he was 'unhurt by the explosion' itself; the script should say he was 'thrown to the ground' or 'knocked down' to be safe. Distance from Hiroshima ground zero: S4 says 'less than a mile and a half' (2.4km), while others say 3km; 'approximately 3 kilometers' is the more common consensus.
